I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS)
Description: The Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS) is sponsored by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau. The MHS produces monthly regional estimates of the average sales price for new manufactured homes and more detailed annual estimates including selected characteristics of new manufactured homes. In addition, MHS produces monthly estimates of homes shipped by status. The statistics on shipments of new manufactured homes are produced by the Institute for Building Technology and Safety (IBTS). They are rounded in the month of release and unrounded in subsequent months. Both not seasonally adjusted and seasonally adjusted annual rates of shipment estimates of new manufactured homes are released monthly.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS)
Description: The Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS) is sponsored by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau. The MHS produces monthly regional estimates of the average sales price for new manufactured homes and more detailed annual estimates including selected characteristics of new manufactured homes. In addition, MHS produces monthly estimates of homes shipped by status. The statistics on shipments of new manufactured homes are produced by the Institute for Building Technology and Safety (IBTS). They are rounded in the month of release and unrounded in subsequent months. Both not seasonally adjusted and seasonally adjusted annual rates of shipment estimates of new manufactured homes are released monthly.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Manufactured Housing Survey comprehensively, starting with several parallel searches.I have a solid foundation. Now let me dig deeper into the FAQ, data products/API access, and the survey's history and users.Let me gather more on the survey's early history, the IBTS role, recent developments, and how the data is used by third parties (FRED, BEA, MHI).I have most of the core material. Let me check the most recent ICR details (burden, costs) and any recent developments or issues affecting the survey.# Research Report: The Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS)

## 0. Verification of the Supplied Description

The description you provided is **accurate and matches the Census Bureau's official program description nearly verbatim**. I confirmed every claim against primary sources (census.gov program pages, the Federal Register, and OMB's reginfo.gov ICR database). A few nuances worth adding for precision:

- The Census Bureau describes itself as both "conducted by" and "collected by" for MHS — the survey is **sponsored (funded) by HUD** and **conducted by the Census Bureau** (reimbursement arrangement, common for Census-conducted surveys on behalf of other agencies under 13 U.S.C. § 8(b)).
- One third-party source (HUD's PD&R Housing & Health Data Dashboard) notes that IBTS-produced shipment statistics are also **republished by the Manufactured Housing Institute (MHI)**, the industry trade association — a useful provenance detail.
- The survey is formally an **OMB-approved information collection under HUD's OMB Control No. 2528-0029**, using Census Form **C-MH-9A**.
- Current status: the survey remains active, with monthly releases continuing (the most recent release I found was dated September 8, 2026, covering data through July 2026), and a 30-day ICR renewal notice published in the *Federal Register* on March 6, 2025.

---

## 1. Identity and Stewardship

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Full name** | Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS); appears in some Census/API contexts as the "Manufactured Homes Survey" |
| **Publisher / collector** | U.S. Census Bureau (Economic Indicators family of programs) |
| **Sponsor** | U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), Office of Policy Development and Research (PD&R) |
| **Shipment statistics producer** | Institute for Building Technology and Safety (IBTS) — a nonprofit that supports HUD's manufactured-housing program; it compiles the list of federally inspected home sections shipped each month, which serves both as the survey's sampling frame and as the basis for the official shipment counts |
| **Republisher** | Manufactured Housing Institute (MHI) republishes shipment data in its industry economic reports |
| **Program page** | census.gov/programs-surveys/mhs |
| **Respondents** | Manufactured home **dealers** (not households or manufacturers) |
| **Response** | **Voluntary** |
| **OMB control number** | 2528-0029 (assigned to HUD/PD&R) |

A distinctive governance feature: this is a *hybrid* product. The **shipment counts** are essentially a census (a tally of all HUD-code home sections reported to IBTS by manufacturers), while the **price, status, and characteristics** estimates come from the Census Bureau's monthly sample survey of dealers.

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

The survey rests on a web of statutes:

- **Title 42 U.S.C. § 5424 note** — from the **Housing and Community Development Act of 1980**, giving the HUD Secretary discretion to ensure the public understands distinctions between types of factory-built housing. This is the basis for HUD collecting and reporting manufactured home sales prices for the nation, Census regions, states, and selected metro areas, and for monitoring whether homes are placed on owned vs. rented lots.
- **Title 13 U.S.C. § 8(b)** — authorizes the Census Bureau to conduct surveys on behalf of other federal agencies (here, HUD).
- **Title 12 U.S.C. § 1701z-1** — HUD's research and demonstration authority.
- **Title 13 U.S.C. § 9** — confidentiality: responses are seen only by sworn Census staff, used only for statistical purposes, and respondent copies are immune from legal process. The Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015 provides additional data-transmission protections.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. ch. 35, § 3507)** — the vehicle for periodic OMB clearance (Federal Register notices, e.g., 2015, 2022, and the March 6, 2025 30-day notice for OMB No. 2528-0029).
- **Housing and Economic Recovery Act (HERA) of 2008, § 2145(b)** — the most concrete downstream mandate: it requires HUD to develop an indexing method to annually adjust Title I manufactured home loan limits. The final rule ("Indexing Methodology for Title I Manufactured Home Loan Limits," published in the *Federal Register* on February 28, 2024) uses single- and double-section price data from MHS to set maximum loan amounts for the Title I Manufactured Home Loan Program (applied to loans applied for on or after March 29, 2024).

## 3. History

- **1959** — the shipments series begins (manufacturer-reported tallies), making the total-shipments series one of the longest continuous housing series in federal statistics.
- **1974** — the survey proper begins, monthly. (1974 also marks the HUD-code era: the Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards.) HUD has funded the survey "since the early 1970s" per the ICR record.
- **1974–1979** — methodology #1: monthly samples of dealers within 137 geographic areas/primary sampling units; dealers reported homes received, placed, and held in inventory.
- **After 1979** — methodology #2: monthly samples of *shipped units*; dealers telephoned each month until the unit was reported "placed."
- **January 2010** — sample redesign, from a 1-in-40 systematic sample to the current fixed-size design.
- **August 2014** — major redesign (methodology #3, still current): dealers are contacted **once, four months after shipment**, to capture status, price, and characteristics. This created a **series break** — data before 2014 ("previous series," 1980–2013) is retained separately and is *not comparable*.
- **January 2021** — questionnaire modifications: identification of **leased** units, better distinction of placed vs. not-yet-placed, and updated characteristics questions aligned with industry standards (another comparability caveat for the annual characteristics series).
- **2024** — the HERA-mandated Title I loan-limit indexing rule takes effect, cementing the survey's regulatory role.
- **2025** — routine OMB reclearance in progress (30-day notice, March 6, 2025).

## 4. Methodology (current series, 2014–present)

- **Target population:** all new manufactured home shipments in the U.S. that have received a federal inspection (HUD-code homes). Modular and other factory-built non-HUD-code homes are *not* covered.
- **Frame:** IBTS's monthly list of new HUD-inspected home sections. Sections shipped to Canadian dealers or FEMA-only dealers are removed from the sampling frame (FEMA units are included with certainty for estimation, but no dealer data are collected for them).
- **Sample:** a systematic sample without replacement, stratified across the four Census regions, fixed at **405 home sections per month** (slightly fewer if duplicate sections of the same home are drawn). A new frame and sample each month.
- **Collection:** a mailed form (C-MH-9A) sent to the receiving dealer **four months after shipment**; response by mail, fax, phone, or the online portal (respond.census.gov/mhs). Collection lasts ~11 business days. Reference period covers the home's status since shipment.
- **Key items:** sales price (actual if sold/placed; *intended* if not yet sold — both are included in the average price estimates), status (sold/placed for residential use; intended for sale for residential use; placed for non-residential use; other, including lost, destroyed, FEMA), size, final destination/location, leased status, titling, length, width, bedrooms.
- **Processing:** hot-deck imputation for missing items (donors matched within imputation cells); weighting with adjustment to population control totals for single- vs. multi-section homes; an adjustment factor for frame sections lacking dealer information.
- **Quality caveats:** voluntary response, a small monthly sample (~405 units) means nontrivial sampling variability — use the published measures of sampling error; and see the revision/rounding practices below.

## 5. Data Products, Coverage, and Access

**What's published and how far back:**

| Series | Geography | Frequency | Begins |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total shipments (NSA and seasonally adjusted annual rate) | U.S. | Monthly | **1959** |
| Shipments by size, shipments to states | U.S., state | Monthly/annual | 2000 (state by size); 1994 (annual state totals) |
| Shipments by status | U.S. | Monthly | Jan 2014 |
| Average sales price by region and size (Total/Single/Double) | U.S., regions | Monthly | 2014 |
| Average sales price | State | Annual | (state-level annual) |
| Selected characteristics of placed homes | Regions | Annual | **1980** |
| Average/median square feet | Regions | Annual | current series |
| **Public Use File (PUF)** — microdata for all sampled homes with weights and imputation flags | — | Annual | 2014 (files now available through 2025) |

**Revision and rounding practices (important for analysts):**
- Shipment figures are **rounded in the month of release and unrounded in subsequent months**; total shipments for the prior two months are revised with each release.
- Monthly by-status and average-price estimates are *not* revised.
- With the April release, **seasonally adjusted shipment estimates are revised for the current year and the previous five years**.

**Access channels:**
- census.gov MHS program pages: monthly press releases, latest data tables, historical tables, previous-series (1980–2013) archive.
- **Census Economic Indicator Time Series (econ_timeseries) tool** for charts and bulk downloads (program codes MHS and MHS2).
- **Census Data API:** `api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/mhs` (historical shipments) and `.../mhs2` (2014–present) — free, but requires an API key.
- **Public Use File** downloads with technical documentation (census.gov/.../MHS/puf.html), enabling custom tabulations and variance estimation.
- **FRED (St. Louis Fed):** the full MHS release is mirrored there (e.g., SHTNSAUS/SHTSAUS — total shipments, NSA/SA, monthly from 1959; average sales price series by size and region from 2014), providing convenient programmatic access and archival stability.

## 6. Typical Users and Uses

Census's respondent-information page and the ICR justifications enumerate the user base:

1. **HUD (the sponsor):** monitors total new housing production and affordability; helps determine fair market values and rents; monitors placement on owned vs. rented lots; and — per the 2024 final rule — computes the statutorily mandated annual index for Title I manufactured home loan limits (directly affecting FHA-insured lending).
2. **Bureau of Economic Analysis:** MHS is an input to estimates of **residential fixed investment in GDP** (NIPA Table 5.4.5; e.g., FRED series A945RC1A027NBEA, private fixed investment in manufactured homes).
3. **Trade associations (notably MHI):** housing market analysis and industry economic reports.
4. **Manufacturers and suppliers:** tracking price and characteristic trends (size mix, single vs. multi-section, features).
5. **Secondary/tertiary users:** academic and Fed researchers (via FRED), lenders, market analysts, journalists, and housing-policy advocates — particularly because manufactured housing is a leading source of unsubsidized affordable housing.
6. **FEMA/disaster-housing analysts:** the survey explicitly tracks FEMA-destination units (e.g., post-hurricane deployments).

## 7. Public Benefit and Policy Significance

- Manufactured housing supplies **much of the low-cost new housing in the U.S.** — per the 2022 ICR justification, over 94,500 new units shipped in 2020, roughly **9% of all new single-family housing**. MHS is the *only* federal statistical product providing comprehensive price, status, and characteristics data on this stock.
- It feeds **GDP** (residential investment), so the macroeconomic accounts depend on it.
- It directly operates a **consumer-protection-adjacent mandate**: annual FHA Title I loan limits for manufactured homes, home lots, and combination loans are now indexed off MHS price data.
- It preserves a **65+ year continuous monthly time series (1959–present)** — invaluable for studying the industry's boom (372,843 shipments in 1998), collapse (~49,789 in 2009), and partial recovery.
- All outputs are **free and public**, including unit-level microdata (PUF) with documentation sufficient for variance estimation — unusually generous for a small economic survey.

## 8. Notes for Preservationists and Data Librarians

- **Series breaks:** three distinct methodological eras (1974–79, 1980–2013, Aug 2014–present) plus a 2021 form change. The 1959+ *shipments* series is continuous, but status/price/characteristics series are not comparable across 2014. The old series is preserved on a dedicated "Previous Series Data" page — worth harvesting independently since it sits outside the current data products.
- **Two API endpoints** (`mhs` vs `mhs2`) reflect the series break; documentation and variables differ.
- **Vintages are not preserved by the Census Bureau** in a public vintage archive for MHS; FRED's companion **ALFRED** preserves vintages of the BEA-derived GDP series but not the raw MHS vintages. If as-released vintages matter (e.g., real-time analysis), the monthly press-release PDFs and FRED download dates are the best available record.
- **Rounding/revision policy** means a value seen in the release month can differ from the final historical table — always cite the final, unrounded series for analysis and note the revision window (2 months for levels; 5+ years for seasonal factors, revised each April).
- **Provenance chain:** raw manufacturer reports → IBTS → Census (sampling frame and shipment counts) → published tables → FRED/MHI redistribution. The IBTS tabulation is *outside* Title 13 (it's administrative data), while dealer responses are Title 13-protected.
- The 2015 ICR put the survey's annual cost at roughly **$404,000** — a small program with outsized downstream use, which is a relevant argument in any continuity/defunding debate.

## 9. Key Sources

- Census Bureau, MHS About/Methodology/FAQ/Information pages: census.gov/programs-surveys/mhs/
- MHS Latest & Previous Series data pages (history of survey program, 1959–present tables)
- Federal Register, *30-Day Notice of Proposed Information Collection: Manufactured Housing Survey; OMB Control No. 2528-0029*, March 6, 2025 (authority, HERA loan-limit indexing, 2024 final rule)
- Federal Register, October 2, 2015 ICR notice (cost, authority)
- reginfo.gov ICR package 202205-2528-002 (OMB clearance history)
- MHS Public Use File documentation (2021) — sampling and estimation detail
- Census Data API discovery pages (timeseries/eits/mhs, mhs2)
- FRED, "Manufactured Housing Survey" release page and BEA NIPA manufactured-homes series
- HUD PD&R Housing & Health Data Dashboard (MHS entry, MHI republication note)

**Bottom line:** MHS is a small, long-running, jointly governed federal survey — HUD-sponsored, Census-conducted, IBTS-fed — that is nonetheless load-bearing for GDP measurement, FHA loan limits, and the study of America's affordable factory-built housing stock, with free access through Census tables, the API, annual microdata (PUF), and FRED. Its main analytical hazards are the 2014 and 2021 series breaks, monthly rounding-then-unrounding, and the rolling revision cycle.

Let me confirm the current ICR approval status and check for any 2026 survey cancellations or MHS-specific threats.# Risk Assessment: Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS)

**Assessment date context:** Research conducted October 2026. Key events since January 2025 include a 43-day federal government shutdown (October–November 2025), major Census Bureau staffing losses and leadership turnover, and deep proposed budget cuts to HUD's research account (MHS's sponsor). Despite all this, the MHS itself has continued publishing monthly, most recently on October 6, 2026, and its annual 2025 microdata was released in June 2026.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- All historical products remain live on census.gov as of this research: latest data tables, historical/supplemental tables back to 1959 (shipments), the "previous series" archive (1980–2013), annual characteristics data (2014–2025, posted June 2026), and annual Public Use Files through 2025 (the 2025 PUF, 4,859 records, approved under CBDRB-FY26-0221) — census.gov/programs-surveys/mhs.html, .../puf.html, .../old-series.html.
- Both Census API endpoints (`timeseries/eits/mhs` and `mhs2`) remain operational, and the econ_timeseries download tool still offers the full series.
- Redundant copies exist and are current: FRED/ALFRED mirror the entire release (SHTNSAUS/SHTSAUS from 1959; price series from 2014), with vintages preserved in ALFRED; MHI republishes shipment data; IBTS holds the administrative source records for shipments.

**Evidence for higher levels:** None found. No reports of removed MHS tables, dropped historical series, or altered past data. The broader "disappearing datasets" problem documented across government (CBPP 9/29/25; Federal News Network 12/2025) has not touched MHS historical products.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** The full historical record — including the pre-2014 previous series, which is the most vulnerable legacy artifact — remains publicly available and unaltered, with robust third-party mirrors.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- Monthly releases have continued without interruption through October 6, 2026 (ALFRED release pages; Census econ_timeseries showing "Release Date October 6, 2026").
- The ICR renewal proceeded on schedule: 60-day notice (Nov. 27, 2024), 30-day notice (March 6, 2025), comments closed April 7, 2025 — ahead of the July 31, 2025 expiration. The respondent portal (respond.census.gov/mhs) affirms active OMB approval (No. 2528-0029) and shows live collection cycles (respondent due dates into September 2026).
- The 2025 annual data and PUF were published on schedule in June 2026.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The government shutdown (lapse in appropriations, Oct.–Nov. 2025) caused missed intended release dates: the November 2025 release slipped from the scheduled November 6 to **November 20, 2025**, and December's release slipped from December 4 to **December 9, 2025**. Census's own historic release-dates file annotates these with "*Due to lapse in appropriations release dates have been revised" (census.gov/programs-surveys/mhs, 2025-releasedates.pdf; historic-release-dates.pdf).
- The release schedule fully recovered in 2026 (Jan. 7, Feb. 5, Mar. 5, Apr. 6, May 6, and monthly releases through Oct. 6, 2026 all on schedule).

**Evidence for higher levels:** None. No skipped collection cycle, no missed statutory deadline, no ICR lapse exceeding one year.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** The intended publication dates were demonstrably missed in November–December 2025 (a rubric criterion for Moderate), driven by an external funding lapse rather than program-specific decisions, and the program has since returned to schedule with an active, timely-renewed ICR.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- Granularity is unchanged: the same monthly series (shipments NSA/SA, shipments by status, average sales price by region and size), state-level annual data, annual characteristics, and annual microdata continue at the same detail. The 2025 PUF sampled 4,859 of a planned ~4,860 homes — the sample design is intact (405 sections/month).
- Frequency is unchanged (monthly + annual), and no content reductions or suppressions have been announced.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- Timeliness was temporarily degraded (2-week and 5-day release slips in Nov.–Dec. 2025, above).
- Emerging risk to timeliness and quality from the producing agency: the Census Bureau lost an estimated **15% of staff since FY24** and roughly **1,300–1,500 employees** to deferred resignations, with ~100 additional RIF notices during the shutdown (AMSTAT "The Nation's Data at Risk 2025"; Bloomberg Law 10/2025; GovExec 7/2025; AP). Commerce contract-approval backlogs exceeded 3,000 requests as of May 2025, and a Commerce OIG evaluation found chronic field-staffing gaps.
- MHS depends on a precise, timing-sensitive pipeline (IBTS frame → 4-month-lag dealer contact → monthly estimation); agency-wide collection disruption is a plausible emerging threat, as seen with other Census surveys (e.g., HTOPS postponements, canceled 2026 governments classification survey — NPR 4/17/25).

**Evidence for higher levels:** None — no reduction in granularity, frequency, or scope has occurred.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** Content and granularity are fully maintained, but there has been an actual (brief) timeliness disruption plus well-documented, ongoing staffing and operational strain at the collecting agency that constitutes an emerging risk to timeliness.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- Statutory authorization is explicitly named and long-standing: 42 U.S.C. § 5424 note (Housing and Community Development Act of 1980), 13 U.S.C. § 8(b), and 12 U.S.C. § 1701z-1 — cited in every ICR notice since at least 2000 (Federal Register, 3/6/2025; 4/27/2000).
- MHS is required for implementation of a federal program with real teeth: **HERA § 2145(b) (2008) mandates annual indexing of FHA Title I manufactured-home loan limits**, and HUD's 2024 final rule explicitly uses MHS single- and double-section price data to set those limits (Federal Register, 2/28/2024; referenced in the 2025 ICR notice).
- No alternative data collection exists for price, placement status, or characteristics of new manufactured homes. The partial substitute — IBTS's administrative shipment tallies (republished by MHI) — covers only counts, and BEA's GDP residential-investment estimates depend on MHS inputs.
- HUD's own FY2026 and FY2027 budget justifications continue to list MHS as part of the "backbone of the Nation's housing data infrastructure" (hud.gov 2026/2027 Congressional Justifications).

**Evidence for higher levels:** The survey is not named in statute itself (it implements statutory purposes), and the shipments component does have a quasi-alternative source — but neither meets the rubric's High Risk bar, which requires substitutability for the collection as a whole.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** Explicit statutory authority, a clear statutory mandate that only these data can fulfill (Title I loan-limit indexing), GDP relevance, and no substitute collection for the survey's core content.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk (multiple criteria met at the producing agencies):**
- **Census Bureau: ≥1,000 staff lost.** Approximately 1,300–1,500 employees lost since January 2025 (deferred resignation/early retirement), ~100 RIF notices in October 2025, and an estimated **15% total staffing loss since FY24** (Bloomberg Law; GovExec; AMSTAT; AP).
- **Leadership removed.** Director Robert Santos departed early (early 2025); political appointee George Cook became acting director in September 2025 while also serving as acting Under Secretary for Economic Affairs — leadership instability explicitly flagged by AMSTAT.
- **Budget cuts ≥20% proposed at the sponsor.** HUD PD&R's Research and Technology account (which funds MHS): FY2026 President's Budget requested $95M vs. $139M FY2025 enacted (a ~22–32% proposed cut; NLIHC analysis; HUD FY26 CJ); FY2027 President's Budget requests **$63M, $59.5M below the FY2026 enacted level (~-49%)** (HUD FY27 CJ). FY2026 enacted (~$122.5M implied by the FY27 CJ) appears to be a ~12% cut from FY2025.
- Census FY2026 budget request: 9% staffing decline from FY24 overall, 2% for current surveys (AMSTAT; C2ER notes possible elimination of "some specialty surveys").

**Evidence for lower levels:**
- MHS itself is a very small line item (roughly $400K/year per the 2015 ICR), fully reimbursed by HUD, and has continued operating without interruption through October 2026 — the specific program team appears functional.
- PD&R headcount is projected roughly flat (138 FTE FY2025 → 137 FY2027 per HUD's FY27 CJ).
- Note: the requested federal staffing tracker (usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) was archived December 31, 2025 and its table data could not be extracted; the AMSTAT and news sourcing above serves as the staffing evidence.

**Selected level: High Risk.** The rubric's thresholds are met at both parent agencies (≥1,000 staff lost and leadership removed at the collector; ≥20% proposed budget cuts at the sponsor), even though the MHS program itself has so far been spared direct cuts.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- No MHS-specific change since January 2025: the 2025 ICR renewal was a routine "Extension of a currently approved collection" with unchanged content and burden (~4,860 responses, ~1,604 hours); no negative policy notes on the MHS site; no Presidential-Action-driven ICR; no content changes aligned to administration priorities.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- **DOGE publicly stated in May 2025 that the Census Bureau's 100+ non-decennial surveys are largely "obsolete" and "not being used to drive any" policy** — an administration-affiliated statement suggesting cuts to exactly the class of small surveys MHS belongs to (Federal News Network, 12/2025).
- Administration posture toward federal statistics is broadly hostile: presidential memorandum altering decennial apportionment, political appointees installed at Census/BEA, and multiple watchdog reports on disappearing datasets and political pressure (CBPP 9/29/25; AP; AMSTAT).
- Actual cancellations/postponements of sibling Census surveys in 2025 (2026 governments classification survey canceled; HTOPS postponed) demonstrate that non-core surveys are being terminated under current policy.
- Mitigating counterweight: the administration's stated housing priorities (deregulation, housing supply, lowering costs) align with manufactured housing's role, and HUD's budget justifications continue to defend MHS.

**Evidence for higher levels:** None — no MHS-specific termination, revision, or negative site notice; no presidential-action-driven changes to this collection.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** No action has been taken against MHS specifically, but administration officials have explicitly floated eliminating "obsolete" non-decennial Census surveys, and comparable surveys have already been canceled — a pending/considered-change environment rather than an implemented one.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

**Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue**
All historical tables, the pre-2014 previous series, PUFs through 2025, and API endpoints remain fully accessible, with independent mirrors (FRED/ALFRED, MHI).

**Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk**
Monthly publication continues on schedule through October 2026 and the ICR was renewed before its July 2025 expiration, but intended release dates were missed in November–December 2025 due to the lapse in appropriations.

**Data Quality: Moderate Risk**
Granularity and frequency are fully maintained and the sample design is intact, but there was an actual temporary timeliness slip, and the Census Bureau's ~15% staffing loss, contract backlogs, and field-staffing gaps pose a documented emerging risk to this survey's tightly timed collection pipeline.

**Statutory Context: No Known Issue**
Explicit statutory authority (42 U.S.C. § 5424 note; 13 U.S.C. § 8(b)); required for implementing the HERA-mandated FHA Title I loan-limit indexing rule (2024); feeds BEA's GDP; no substitute data collection exists for its core content.

**Staffing and Funding: High Risk**
Census Bureau has lost ~1,300–1,500 staff (≥1,000) with director-level leadership turnover; HUD PD&R's funding account has faced proposed cuts of 22–49% in the FY2026 and FY2027 President's Budgets — even though the small MHS program itself has so far continued uncut.

**Policy: Moderate Risk**
No MHS-specific changes since January 2025 and the ICR renewal was routine, but DOGE's public designation of non-decennial Census surveys as "obsolete," the cancellation of sibling surveys, and broader administration pressure on statistical agencies create a credible, pending threat environment.

**Overall reading:** MHS is a low-visibility, low-cost, legally well-anchored survey that has so far weathered the 2025–2026 turmoil with only a brief shutdown-driven release delay. Its principal vulnerabilities are institutional rather than program-specific: the degraded staffing and leadership at the Census Bureau and the deep proposed cuts to HUD's research account. The strongest mitigants are the HERA loan-limit mandate, the absence of any substitute data source, the dataset's full redundancy on FRED/ALFRED, and its explicit defense in HUD's own budget justifications. A preservationist's priority actions would be archiving monthly release vintages (Census does not preserve MHS vintages publicly; ALFRED covers only the FRED-carried series) and monitoring the FY2027 PD&R appropriation and the next ICR cycle (due ~2028).
